speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Recognising the growing importance of electronic transactions, especially e-commerce, Singapore was the first country to adopt the Model Law on Electronic Commerce of 1996 or the MLEC, by the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law or UNCITRAL.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The ETA has also facilitated the Government’s use of electronic documents in its engagements with businesses and citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The ETA was repealed and re-enacted in 2010 to adopt the United Nations Convention on the Use of Electronic Communications in International Contracts or the ECC.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The ECC provisions were updated for application to Internet technologies and to harmonise international laws on electronic transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, electronic transactions and e-commerce underpin the global economy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The digital economy is key to the next phase of Singapore’s growth, and our efforts to emerge stronger from the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our strategies include enhancing our digital infrastructure and frameworks, strengthening our citizens’ and businesses’ digital capabilities, and collaboration with international partners.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This Bill will ensure that our legal and regulatory infrastructure keeps pace with international trade law and the latest technological developments so that Singapore remains globally competitive.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Bill was drafted after extensive consultations with stakeholders over several years.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It aims to facilitate faster and more secure transactions while enhancing businesses' and citizens' trust in digitalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, to meet the digitalisation needs of citizens and businesses while introducing adequate safeguards; and second, to ensure that the international harmonisation and technology neutrality of our laws relating to electronic transactions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Model Law enables the creation and use, domestically and internationally, of electronic forms of transferable documents or instruments, otherwise known as Electronic Transferable Records, or ETRs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Transferable documents or instruments entitle the rightful holder to claim the performance of the obligation indicated, such as the delivery of goods or payment of money, and to transfer the right to performance by transferring the document or instrument.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These transferable documents are instruments are used extensively in international trade in industries such as shipping, logistics and finance.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: A bill of lading is used in maritime trade as a transport document and as a document of title over goods in transit.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The seller will engage a carrier to deliver the cargo and will in turn receive a bill of lading from the carrier.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The seller will generally only release the bill of lading to the buyer on payment and the buyer can only collect the goods from the ship by producing the bill of lading.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Often financing is involved and the bill of lading will pass through many parties from the seller to his export bank, then to the buyer's import bank, and eventually to the buyer who may even sell the cargo to a sub-buyer while its cargo is enroute.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The final buyer will have to produce the bill of lading to take delivery of the cargo at the port.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Sometimes, goods arrive at their port of destination before the documents have been processed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In such instances, there will be additional costs to either hold the cargo or to secure a letter indemnifying the carrier for delivering the goods without a bill of lading.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Fraud is a real risk because paper bills of lading can be forged.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Significant resources are therefore required to process paper documents and verify their authenticity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This means considerable time and costs are attributed not only to the actual transportation of the goods, but also to the administrative cost of cargo holding and document processing.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With electronic bills of lading, the transmission of documents will be instantaneous and time spent on verification and rectifying areas will be reduced.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With digital authentication technologies such as digital signatures, centralised ledgers or blockchain, electronic bills of lading also improve security against forgeries.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Commercially available technology solutions for an electronic bill of lading based on contractual frameworks already offer many of these benefits for shippers today.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For example, last year, Singapore-based Ocean Network Express announced that it had used an electronic bill of lading using the S-docks system in a successful shipment of synthetic rubber from Russia to China.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: While this contractual approach benefits the parties to such a contractual framework, it does not affect third parties that are not part of the framework.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: One commercial advantage in using an electronic bill of lading enabled by clause 6 is that a trade financing bank can obtain collateral security over the electronic bill of lading which is legally equivalent to a paper bill of lading.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This may allow the bank to obtain a regulatory capital relief in respect of its trade finance exposure and to pass some of the benefits to its clients in the form of lower fees.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ultimately, end consumers tend to benefit from the lower costs of legal documentation, transportation and trade financing.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As with any digital technology, we need appropriate safeguards to ensure the transactions can be executed with confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The technological and legal challenges of establishing what constitutes an original document and its possession in an electronic environment are key impediments to the use of electronic versions of transferable documents or instruments.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Technological advancements have made it possible to meet these requirements and to prevent the unauthorised duplication of an original document with strong safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Existing commercial electronic bill of lading solutions from the providers such as Bolero and S-docks, as well as newer digital utilities such as IMDA's TradeTrust have demonstrated that stakeholders can use electronic bills of lading with trust through the use of title registries, blockchain and advanced encryption standards and firewalls.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These technologies help to reliably establish the control of the singular electronic bill of lading while ensuring document veracity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Indeed, the industry itself is confident of the use of these technologies as evinced by the International Group of Protection and Indemnity Clubs, providing an equal level of marine liability cover for both paper bills of lading and carriage of cargo under certain electronic bills of lading systems.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The new 16F to 16I set out specific requirements that an electronic record must meet in order to be recognised under the ETA as the electronic functional equivalent of a paper transferable document or instrument.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The functional equivalence rules apply to writing, signature, transferable document, or instrument and possession.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The new sections 16J to 16L set out further functional equivalence rules for requirements relating to the use of ETRs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Specifically, section 16H provides that an electronic record is the electronic functional equivalent of a paper-based transferable document or instrument if several specific requirements are met.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, the electronic record must contain the information required to be contained in the paper transferable document or instrument.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, a reliable method is used to identify that electronic record as the authoritative electronic record constituting the ETR.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Third, that reliable method renders that electronic record capable of being subject to control from the time it is created until it ceases to have any effect or validity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Fourth, that reliable method must retain the integrity of the electronic record.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, these give effect to the singularity requirement which requires reliable identification of the ETR that entitles the holder to request performance of the obligation indicated in it and avoids multiple claims.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Section 16I provides that the legal requirement for the possession of a transferable document or instrument is met with respect to an ETR if a reliable method is used to establish exclusive control of the ETR by a person, and to identify that person as the person in control.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Where this requirement is met, the person in control of an ETR will be in the same legal position as the person in possession of an equivalent paper-based transferable document or instrument.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The new section 16O also sets out a general standard to assess the reliability of each of the methods referred to in the functional equivalence provisions I listed earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In the event of a dispute, it is for the Court to assess the reliability of the method in question, taking into account the non-exhaustive list of relevant circumstances set out the same section.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With the adoption of the MLETR in the new part 2A of the amended ETA, clause 8 of the Bill will remove item 2 relating to transferable documents or instruments from the Exclusion List.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Government is studying the feasibility of removing the remaining items from the Exclusion List bearing in mind the benefits that could accrue to our citizens and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These items will be removed from the Exclusion List when the necessary legislative and regulatory frameworks and corresponding safeguards have been put in place.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The MLETR is an internationally harmonised legal framework developed by UNCITRAL, the core legal body of the UN in international trade law, as a uniform model law recommended for adoption by all jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Model Law facilitates the cross-border use of ETRs, especially when adopted broadly by countries.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Moving forward, as more countries incorporate the MLETR into their domestic law, it will greatly promote cross-border transactions and Singapore's early adoption of the Model Law will strengthen our position as a global commercial hub.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It provides that an ETR is not to be denied legal effect solely on the ground that it was issued or used outside Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The question that then arises is what happens if a cross-border trade involves jurisdictions which do not yet support the use of ETRs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This provides parties with the confidence to use ETRs which are typically transferred multiple times, knowing that a subsequent transferee can choose to convert an ETR to a physical form.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In other words, the provisions are intended to accommodate the use of different technologies, such as traditional registries, tokens and distributed ledgers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Coupled with our close partnerships with sectoral agencies like MPA, Customs, MAS and the industry to develop the eco-system for ETRs, and efforts to promote global adoption of the MLETR through various digital economy agreements, these amendments will further enhance Singapore's position as a global digital economy and bring opportunities and benefits to our businesses and our people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For one, the year 2020 heralded the start of digital transformation journey for many people in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On this note, I applaud the introduction of the amendment Bill as a timely and impactful step towards our Smart Nation journey.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In fact, I would see this amendment as a catch up because the technological solutions are readily available, the people's will and attention to this, the willingness to try it out, are also available now and now it is the legal catch up.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And so, this is yet another piece to the puzzle.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is an industry that has been unduly burdened by tonnes of paperwork for conveying goods across seas.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Earlier, Minister would have illustrated this with many examples and details, so I would just be reinforcing some of these.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The impact of digitising bills of lading in Singapore would be very significant given that seaborne trade has been a critical lifeline of the country ever since Sir Stamford Raffles transformed Singapore into a bustling trade port back in 1819.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With an extensive connection to 600 ports in over 120 countries and more than 130,000 vessels calling on Singapore, the decision to embark on the digitalisation of paper bills of lading is apparent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Apart from	the	enhancement	of	cost	savings	and	data accuracy and perhaps even preventing fraud, digitalisation helps to promote environmental sustainability.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The International	Air	Transport Association (IATA)	introduced digitalisation of air waybills for the airfreight industry about 10 years ago.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On this note, I am heartened that the Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) is the one of the first legal document to be digitalised, which is timely in view of the increasing awareness and acceptance of LPA.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moving forward, the number of registrations is poised to grow further with newer generations of Singaporeans joining the ranks of seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This group of seniors will be technologically savvy, digitally proficient and more receptive of registering for a LPA.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Furthermore, we could open a bank account today on a mobile application through SingPass – MyInfo for authentication, doing away the need to physically step foot into the branch.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These changes will enhance citizens' access to important services.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Prior to this, I had wanted to ask the Minister whether there will be plans to further digitalise other transactions and recognise digital signatures for more legal documents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: That said, as digital solutions increasingly become available and transactions made easier with digitalisation, I would also urge the Government to constantly review and ensure that legal and process safeguards are in place to prevent abuse, especially for transactions that interact or intersect with ordinary citizens' lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Technology is just an enabler, but the process design I think it is very key.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, in terms of inauthenticity as well as doing away with duplicates, blockchain, for example, could solve it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But, sometimes, how do we prevent someone with an agenda from masquerading as someone who he is not, and taking advantage of the process and the convenience of digital solutions?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I think this is something that we will have to always bear in mind, to constantly review and make sure that the safeguards are in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To the extent that these amendments represent the Government's on-going efforts to renew as well as support the modernisation of various areas of the economy – and in this specific case, with regard to trade – it is undeniably welcome and will further bolster our position as a global trading hub.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While such laws that enhance trade facilitation may seem pedestrian, they represent important steps to ensure that less glamorous bread-and-butter aspects of international trade are brought into the 21st century and represent low hanging fruit insofar as gaining efficiencies from digitalisation are concerned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, I wish to just add three points about moves to incorporate blockchain technologies to caution that the remaining excluded items could still be a binding constraint to fully realising efficiency in trade and to stress the need to provide support for our smaller firms as they make this important digital transition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Paragraph 1 in Article 10 of the Model Law was written with the recognition of the inherent difficulty in ascertaining the uniqueness of any given document in an electronic environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In many ways, this is a purely technical issue and one not easily finessed by the language of the law.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, recent innovations in blockchain technology now offer the promise of decentralised assurance of transactions integrity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I note that the amendments only propose to delete item 2 of the First Schedule and these are items excluded by the Electronic Transactions Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Although it may seem sensible to proceed linearly and delete the other items when related legislation is ready, it is worth recognising that these other items may be less unrelated than they may seem prima facie.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For instance, item 4, excludes from the Act the sale, and item 5, the conveyance of immovable property.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But real world trade is executed alongside a very rich set of trade financing instruments, which include not just standard, fair letters of credit, but also other subtler forms of financing such as leasing or inventory financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To the extent that such instruments are still represented on the First Schedule, digitally-enabled trade transactions may potentially remain partially inhibited until these items are ultimately removed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And will these funds be applicable not just to new transactions, but also to enable the digitalisation of the existing stock of paper records for these firms?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Beyond rolling SME support into existing policy, is there a way to ensure that cost savings that accrue from this digitalisation effort are then passed on through to the firms themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One practical way forward, is to endow a Government secretariat, possibly within IMDA's own Digital Tech Hub or Go Digital platform that would assist small business owners in filling up standardised trade documents as a pre-approved solution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another practical suggestion would be for IMDA to maintain a database of accredited shipping or trade legal firms that are familiar with the new digital records standards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This would not only allow the all important demonstration effect, but also enable IMDA to learn the best practices and standard operating procedures necessary for scaling up their assistance and to enable a more systematic evaluation of the costs and benefits of digitalised trading operations for small firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding these three issues, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My focus is on the legal recognition of the digital form of the Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It allows applications and amendments to be made to the LPA safely and conveniently.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As Singaporeans live longer, more people will spend their later years in weaker health.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This can create conflict in a family where their loved one whose mental capacity is temporarily or permanently impaired.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Despite the importance of an LPA, the take-up rate is still very low.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is the largest percentage compared to all other eligible age groups.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I must emphasise that LPA is not just for the elderly, but also for every adult with sound mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The physical nature of the process involves multiple parties, including a doctor or lawyer to sign the documents in person.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is one of the challenges that puts people off the process.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will attract more people to sign up.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, we must ensure that there is an underlying system in place, to enable the required parties to certify the documents online.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, if doctors have access to the patient's medical history, this will help them with their assessment of the patient's mental condition when issuing the LPA.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: LPA goes hand-in-hand with Advanced Care Planning, or ACP.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: LPA applicants should have the option on the application to select their preferred organisations to handle their ACP, and exercise the necessary financial planning.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we look into streamlining this as part of digitalising the LPA?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we also explore possibilities for regular updates and reviews of LPA appointments and ACP wishes online?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should take this opportunity to fundamentally review the LPA application backend processes, adopt a systemic approach and introduce changes accordingly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to do more than changing the physical to digital.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Only then can we move the needle and make a real social impact.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill will adopt, with modifications, the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Transferable Records.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This allows the recognition of electronic records of trade documents at international ports and supports our digitalisation efforts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three clarifications on the Bill and on Singapore's efforts to move towards electronisation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the effectiveness of national digitalisation in international trade with other countries at varying stages of digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Any single transaction in international trade is likely to involve multiple parties in various jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will be important for all parties involved to be certain that electronic documents will be legally valid and enforceable in jurisdictions where the documents may be needed to be enforced.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While Singapore's adoption of the Model Law will make Singapore one of the first mover countries, the current low rate of uptake may mean that electronic trade documents recognised in Singapore may not similarly be recognised abroad.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister had addressed this point earlier, but could I ask whether we working with other countries to provide assurances that electronic trade documents will similarly receive recognition abroad?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on electronically signed deeds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During the circuit breaker period, electronic execution of contracts became much more common practice.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, deeds remain one category of documents where it is unclear if electronic signatures may be accepted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lawyers generally advise against signing deeds using electronic signatures because of the risk that deeds governed by Singapore law or signed in Singapore may not be enforceable if signed using electronic signatures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, the explanatory statement to the Bill makes clear that the adoption of the Model Law and the inclusion of trade documents under the Electronic Transactions Act is part of a wider initiative by the Government to support the electronisation of documents and transactions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As part of IMDA's consultations in 2019, IMDA proposed removing the exclusion of Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, it is proposed that electronic LPA should be allowed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill explains that these other transactions, such as LPAs, will be deleted when the legislative and administrative frameworks supporting electronisation are ready to be implemented.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that an Office of the Public Guardian Online Electronic System is in the works to allow LPAs to be registered electronically.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share how it is working with MSF to ensure that the needs of the elderly are taken into account when rolling out the Electronic System?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to consider that they might not be familiar or comfortable with such a system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While LPAs are of course not only for the elderly, they are a significant population that will make use of this instrument.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should ensure that any Electronic System caters to their needs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also declare my interests as a member of the Institute of Mental Health's Visitors' Board and as an Office of Public Guardian pro bono donee appointed by the Court under the Mental Capacity Act.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the amendment Bill which will bring trade documents within the scope of the Electronic Transactions Act (ETA).

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most maritime trade now uses paper copies of bills of lading.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A single transaction can involve hundreds of pages for such bills.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However as digitalised trade documents can be duplicated easily, financiers, banks must be careful and put up additional measures to prevent double-financing.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the amendments, the ETA will adopt most of the standards of the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law, which sets out an internationally recognised legal framework for electronic records.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Being aligned with the international system for electronic documentation is crucial for us as a global trading and shipping hub.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Presently, banks only finance international trade documents based on signed paper documents.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the amendments, am I correct to understand that electronic signatures will be recognised legally?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As domestic online purchases have surged in recent years, especially for the last one year, can we also look into allowing digitalised delivery notes for local delivery to be recognised as legitimate too?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: LPA forms have to be witnessed and certified by an LPA certificate issuer, who are limited to a medical practitioner accredited by the Public Guardian, a practicing lawyer or a registered psychiatrist.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This means that in effect, all the data entries, signatures and submissions have to be done in the offices of these professionals.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am particularly concerned about the administrative, hardware and software support for the medical practitioners.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding the abovementioned queries, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the amendments, trade documents will be included.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will enable digital documentation with international ports, leading to shorter processing time, reduced costs and hopefully, lowered risks of fraud.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These changes will have a significant impact on shipping and global trade.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a maritime and trading hub, we will definitely benefit from the resultant efficiency and productivity gains.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At this point, I seek the Minister's assurance that we have the digital infrastructural support and cyber expertise to ensure that the cyber fraud risks are minimised.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would he elaborate upon the measures we have in place to protect the integrity of such digital documents?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will be helpful for those who struggle with digitalisation, especially the elderly and underprivileged.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is also important to provide training and guidance for people who intend to make their LPAs online.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Training should be very personal and one-to-one, so that they can ask questions and feel assured.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There should be a one-stop venue where people can make appointments to be guided and advised.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can we seek the support of the SG Digital Ambassadors to help in this initiative and also draw upon the community to assist?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, would cybersecurity measures be introduced to protect the LPA databases, guard against hacking and fraudulent submissions?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):    I would like to ask if there are plans to continue to accept hard copies of LPAs, even after digitalising LPAs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will be helpful for those who struggle with digitalisation, especially the elderly and underprivileged.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is also important to provide training and guidance for people who intend to make their LPAs online.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Training should be very personal and one-to-one, so that they can ask questions and feel assured.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There should be a one-stop venue where people can make appointments to be guided and advised.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, would cybersecurity measures be introduced to protect the LPA databases, guard against hacking and fraudulent submissions?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can we seek the support of SG Digital Ambassadors to help in this initiative and also draw upon the community to assist?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I first declare my interest as a practising international trade and shipping lawyer.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore is one of the busiest international maritime hubs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most of maritime trade involves the use of physical bills of lading which can be cumbersome and voluminous.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With physical bills of lading, there is also a higher possibility and propensity of fraud being perpetrated.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a lawyer, I have been personally involved in many cases concerning litigation disputes on competing claims or contradicting bills of lading and frauds committed upon consignees or trade financing banks.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, having electronic bills of lading or electronic negotiable instruments would clear up this area.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This legislation, together with the Government's Networked Trade Platform (NTP) which is a one-stop trade and logistics eco-system, shall assist Singapore to be a leading trade, supply chain and trade financing hub.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will be able to cut costs and streamline processes of trade financing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Digitalisation means faster processing, lower risks and lower risks of fraud.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Innovative technology like blockchain or smart contracts can further supplement our foray into digitalisation; bringing with it, not only costs and time efficiency, but more convenience and greater confidence in our system.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the area of shipping and international trade, this amendment Bill signifies an important step which will allow Singapore to further enhance its position as a maritime and trade hub.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the various changes and developments to be expected in this area, I hope that the Minister can consider a thorough public awareness campaign, perhaps through industry leaders or trade associations and chambers of commerce, so that businesses especially small and medium enterprises or those that have yet to embark on the digitalisation journey, so that they can too take full advantage of these digital alternatives to trade documents and the specific requirements for electronic records to be recognised.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the Explanatory Statement of this amendment Bill, it is stated that the other matters in the First Schedule will be deleted when the legislative and administrative frameworks supporting the electronisation of those other items are ready to be enacted or implemented.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For these other matters, I think most families would welcome the impending deletion of Items 1 and 3 of the First Schedule regarding the creation or execution of a will and trust or power of attorney, which would include lasting powers of attorney or LPA.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, an LPA must be in hard copy form.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Digitalisation would also allow deputies appointed under LPAs to file their reports online and make it more convenient and faster for deputies to manage the affairs of the donor, like sending an electronic copy of the LPA to third parties, like banks.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For banks or any third parties, they would also have confidence in the transaction as they will be receiving the most up-to-date electronic copy of the LPA from the Office of the Public Guardian.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given our ageing population and the current pandemic situation which limits face-to-face and physical interactions, it is important for us to expedite the digitalisation of such documents, LPAs and wills for our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In short, I am asking for the estimated time of arrival, or ETAs, on the LPAs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With that Mr Speaker, Sir, suggestions and clarifications notwithstanding, I support this Bill.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am Chairman of SISTIC.com, an SME, Independent Director of SPH, Council Member of Singapore Business Federation and Deputy Chairman of SBF Foundation, and a former IBM Managing Director of IBM Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: If you would, allow me to make a couple of points to address the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-Charge of Trade Relations’ proposed amendments to the Electronic Transactions Act.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, I start by saying this is my maiden speech and I support the Bill, which is the reason why I am up here.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: If you would allow me, I would just like to remind us that one of the key things is to create the future, we must understand the past.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When I read the Bill, the first thing goes back to 1985 when Singapore first launched TradeNet.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Looking back at the past, we always must have the lessons from our journey so far and develop our collective response to the opportunities and challenges ahead of us to ensure that Singapore 2.0 will be even better than 1.0, for ourselves and for our children and future generations to come.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, as the past year has taught us, we learnt to be resilient in the wake of disruptions like the COVID-19 pandemic, to expect the unexpected, to learn from past experiences like SARS and the Global Financial Crisis, while at the same time stay alert to constant changes, be agile and adapt as we go along, and most importantly, to strengthen our resolve for collective response to emerge stronger post-COVID-19 even as we are being tested at every level, every day.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It will be remiss of me not to take this opportunity, as this is my first time, to thank everyone in the House for all that you have done to lead and will continue to lead us safely and thoughtfully through these unprecedented times.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, special mention to the WOG or whole-of-Government Taskforce at every level and to our essential workers in the front line.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As Singaporeans and residents, we are all grateful.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has always led with a vision, rallied Singaporeans and the community to work towards the common goal, and execute together, to make it a reality.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his team rallied Singaporeans with the vision to take Singapore from “Third World to First”; “from mudflat to metropolis”.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And our Prime Minister Mr Lee Hsien Long in his National Day Rally Speech of 2014, has yet again set in motion, our transformation agenda to becoming the world’s first smart nation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I feel so humbled to have the opportunity to be here in this very Chamber where these visions and strategies for Singapore were and are being charted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore’s success lies in our collective ability to execute and I have no doubt that once again, even with this Bill and amongst others, we will do the same.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We are in an era of "acceleration of digital”.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The coronavirus pandemic has propelled technology to the forefront of business agendas, and into the lives of everyone.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Work-From-Home, Home-Based Learning, SafeEntry, TraceTogether and SingPass have become common vocabulary amongst Singaporeans and residents.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have all personally experienced during the last 12 months, the surge of e-commerce, the convenience of online food delivery, the proliferation of Zoom meetings and online webinars, and for me personally, K-dramas and masses crash-landed into my living room.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, acceleration to digital “everything” is on a different trajectory.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Government support has been and continues to be vital toward recovery with 47% and 31% reporting that help with talent and building capabilities respectively, were very relevant.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Other technology adoption challenges which they spelt out include the upskilling of staff, expensive licensing of IP, cyber security risks and lack of management expertise to drive technology change.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For more information on the survey results, please refer to SBF.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I highlighted these more specifics, related to their digitalisation challenges.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: By contrast, so that we do not think that we are that bad, Singapore’s MNCs in the IT and professional services sectors and the LLCs in Financial Services sector had outperformed their peers globally.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, the good news is that even for the SMEs, it did improve and increase from 2019 to 2020.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has given us a succinct proposition for why the amendments to the Electronic Transaction Act.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In my past life at IBM, I was involved with the Maersk and IBM TradeLens project as well as initiating the PIL and IBM electronic bill of lading pilot.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We saw reduced time and reduced costs for trade document processing, and transactions were more secure, inter-operable, and transparency and provenance was built into the system.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that the Bill for the Electronic Transactions (Amendment) Bill is very timely as the outlook for digital trade and digital services is rapidly growing.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The lack of regulation and legislation globally does increase costs and risks for all.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: New rules are needed in the digital economy, and it is certainly far better to be co-writing the rules then to be playing catch up.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That said, we are cognisant that COVID-19 has exacerbated the divide between the "haves" and "have nots".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen during the circuit breaker that access to computers and high-speed wifi for students to take part in home-based learning cannot be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, for our SMEs, their ability to effectively participate and leverage the trade platforms created for their benefit, cannot be assumed.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the following suggestions I am going to make, are already being considered and so I beg your indulgence.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But certainly, it is because of the network effect.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Innovation in business models, policies, regulation, technology and the development of skills all go hand-in-hand.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The second is SMEs lack the skills and the management leadership and expertise to drive digital transformation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The lack of leadership expertise to drive this transformation is one of their challenges.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One suggestion or thought, is for the Government to consider seconding some of their tech scholars to work in SMEs or SME sectors, on these digital transformation efforts.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And leveraging on the Electronic Transactions (Amendment) Bill is definitely a good one to go with.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our businesses have enquired about when we will have “SignNow” so that companies can use e-signatures on banking documents and comply with the banks’ compliance process.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And I believe several speakers ahead of me have mentioned this.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We need on-going dialogue among the stakeholders to listen to each other, to better understand the issues and find the solutions together.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To conclude, I hope that we can take this unprecedented time of chaos caused by a health pandemic, to forge ahead on how we might have an integral development approach to growth where we collectively – Government, big corporations, large enterprises, the well-endowed, civil society, IHLs, together with the SMEs – bring all the SMEs along, bring those who feel that they are marginalised and disadvantaged, along.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The only criteria is that the SMEs and their teams are themselves hungry to survive and to grow, and have the conviction and the resolve to transform.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To get on to the digital train, there are investments to be made, and if you see the list of challenges which I shared earlier, the work to get them on the digital track must be now.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It has been my experience any laws, policies and programmes on digitalisation never fail to elicit very wide-ranging views and suggestions, all given and with the best of intentions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I hope Members will understand if I confine my response to the issues that are germane to this particular Bill and some of the immediate adjacencies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I also like to assure them that some of the other areas will be looked into by the respective agencies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to start by agreeing fully with all Members the fact that digitalisation and indeed this Bill, are all but enablers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And ultimately, it is how these enablers help to improve the lives of our citizens and opportunities for our businesses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is the ultimate lens through which we should be looking at this and many of the other initiatives.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And in that spirit, I want to thank Members for their various questions and comments on the key issues that this Bill seeks to address.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In particular, if I were to condense it, the views fall into two broad themes, namely: what are we doing to ensure that businesses digitalise in a sustainable and effective manner; and secondly, what are we doing to enhance and protect consumers' quality of experience related to electronic transactions?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some Members have asked about the cost impact to businesses arising from the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Beyond replacing paper documents with electronic transferrable records or ETRs, businesses that wish to unlock the full potential of digital solutions will have to invest resources into reviewing their existing operations, IT and digital infrastructures and systems and their business processes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Members have noted, today's predominantly paper-based trading environment does incur in inefficiencies and delays because the time required to process paper documents may far exceed, in some instances, that needed to physically move the goods.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, ETRs, such as electronic bills of lading can yield significant savings cost savings across the entire cost value chain.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Although Ms Janet Ang highlighted, there may be a transition period when businesses have to work with both electronic and paper-based bills of lading, because their business partners may not be ready to adopt electronic bills of lading, the overall long-term benefits and competitive advantages remain compelling.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ultimately, individual businesses must weigh the costs and benefits for themselves.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about how the amendments will ensure that Singapore continues to be interoperable with the global trade eco-system, especially when many countries have yet to adopt the use of ETRs widely.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Its text was formulated at the UNCITRAL Working Group meetings, attended by delegates who represented the views and interests of countries from all over the world.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As a Model Law, the MLETR text provides a suggested framework for lawmakers in national Governments to consider adopting as part of their domestic legislation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the long run, as countries move forward to adopt the MLETR, these amendments will naturally confer a certain degree of international harmonisation with other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But not every country will be ready to enact the Model Law in the near future.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Hence, the new sections 16M and 16N contain substantive provisions that enable the change of medium from an ETR to a physical transferable document or instrument, and vice versa.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This enables parties to decide to use an ETR with the assurance that the ETR can be converted to a physical transferable document or instrument at some later stage in the life cycle, and can be converted back to an ETR, if needed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have also been working on Digital Economy Agreements, which is really a digital analogue of Free Trade Agreements.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And through these agreements, we hope to foster the global adoption of the Model Law, and encourage the global trade industry to use ETRs with confidence via a common legal framework.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Members will recall that we have signed two such Digital Economy Agreements, one with Australia, and one with Chile and New Zealand.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, this will be another part of our effort to promote the adoption of this Model Law thereby realising the network benefits that many Members have mentioned.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked about our efforts to encourage industry to adopt ETR solutions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Apart from legal reforms, Singapore is actively working with our industry and international partners to develop the digital trade eco-system.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In doing so, it enables interoperability across digital platforms so that electronic trade documents can be exchanged in a trusted fashion while ensuring document authenticity, proof of provenance and transfers of title for ETRs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have made good progress in the development of TradeTrust since the signing of our partnership with the International Chamber of Commerce and 17 major corporations, such as MasterCard, PSA International and Standard Chartered at Davos last year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This goes to the point that Mr Louis Ng raised about how we are promoting the use of such technology.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I think it is important to note that the SMEs will stand to benefit from TradeTrust.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, in some ways, perhaps even more so, and not just large organisations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is a good starting point for tech firms in the business of providing products or services around ETRs, while enabling them to be interoperable without additional cost.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Businesses of all sizes throughout the entire value chain involved in cross-border trade, stand to benefit from TradeTrust, as electronic trade documents, including ETRs can be transferred in a seamless and secure manner.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Additionally, IMDA partners Trade Associations and Chambers have been reaching out to SMEs through webinars and industry events to help SMEs better understand the benefits of digitalisation as well as the different Government support that is available.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: IMDA's SME Digital Tech Hub provides specialist digital technology advisory to SMEs that have advanced digital needs, such as data analytics and cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked how this syncs with the broader effort by MTI in terms of promoting the adoption of such technologies by SMEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Broadly speaking, we have a digitalisation effort which all Government agencies, in particular, our economic agencies are working on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is an effort that we undertake in partnership with industry partners, Trade Associations and Chambers and international partners, in the manner I have just described.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In doing this, our objective is to not just pursue technology for the sake of technology, but to ensure that it is assessed through the eyes of industry to ensure that there is value.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because, as we have all agreed, that is the ultimate objective that it derives benefit and it is a means to an end.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, our objective is not so much about picking platforms or picking technologies but it is about ensuring that our system remains open, interoperable, allowing for the fact that technology may evolve over time and therefore, we need dexterity in our system that allows that compatibility across current and new technologies, and indeed, current technologies that may be co-existing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Tin Pei Ling asked about the issue of the sufficiency of safeguards for ETRs and digital transactions, and how the Government will ensure the integrity and authenticity of these newer forms of electronic transferable documents or instruments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are legal safeguards in place for the creation and use of ETRs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Don Wee will be glad to know that these provisions collectively serve to prevent the unauthorised replication of an ETR by an ETR management system.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The new section 16O which sets out a general reliability standard for the assessment of the reliable methods used to give effect to the requirements in new Part IIA, also includes factors, such as the "assurance of data integrity" and "the security of hardware and software".

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In terms of technological safeguards, there have been significant advancements which enable us to transact in an even more secure and seamless manner.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Distributed ledger technology, smart contracts and biometrics are just some examples of the rapidly evolving areas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These technologies, along with transparent electronic audit trails, will help prevent the tampering of data by third parties.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We must all do our part to acquire the skills to protect our digital resources from cybersecurity risks.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Government is committed to the security and resilience of Singapore's cyberspace and to protect our critical information infrastructure.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Businesses on that part must create a cyber secure environment for their business and customers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: CSA launched the Safer Cyberspace Masterplan, which lays out the detailed steps that organisations can take to protect themselves from cyber risks.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As they introduce ETR solutions, business owners should review their cyber risk assessments because the digital footprint grows in tandem and they must implement proactive measures to protect their businesses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Don Wee asked for clarifications with regard to the circumstances in which electronic signatures may be used and Ms Janet Ang provided suggestions to facilitate use of electronic signatures.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Essentially, the ETA today allows electronic signatures to be used in place of physical signatures, but this does not cover matters under the Exclusion List, including transferable documents or instruments.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For Excluded Matters, it may still be possible to use electronic signatures in circumstances permitted under the Common Law.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I would advise parties to consult their lawyers for guidance on this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Louis Ng spoke about signing deeds electronically.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Currently, the formalities for executing a deed depend on whether there are requirements prescribed in the legislation governing the subject matter of the deed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Where the legislation is silent, then a deed must be executed according to the principles established at common law.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In other words, it must be sealed and delivered.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We understand that deeds are also commonly witnessed in practice.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Such formalities are safeguards developed over time to provide a measure of reliability and security.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is necessary to consider whether and what safeguards are needed if, in fact, we want to migrate these deeds to the electronic domain, in other words, to digitalise them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this is an area of work that MinLaw and other relevant Ministries are studying.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to now address the issues pertaining to consumers’ quality of experience related to electronic transactions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have shared how the Bill will enable the use of ETRs, such as electronic bills of lading, to reduce the cost of shipping, streamline workflows, resulting in a more efficient global logistics network.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: While the direct benefits of the amendments primarily impact businesses, individuals could ultimately enjoy lower prices of goods as a result of the reductions in transaction costs associated with faster documentation processing, transportation and trade financing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling and Mr Zhulkarnain asked about our future plans to digitalise other transactions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When an item is feasible for digitalisation, the Government will work towards the implementation of the necessary legislative and regulatory frameworks and corresponding safeguards.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The progressive removal of items from the Exclusion List will send a strong signal that Singapore remains committed to be a leading digital economy and a secure and trusted hub for e-commerce and other forms of electronic transactions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It will also reinforce the Government’s wider digitalisation effort and facilitate the achievement of the Digital Government Blueprint to provide end-to-end digital options for most Government services.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, MSF’s forthcoming Mental Capacity (Amendment) Bill will introduce, amongst other things, a framework to enable and safeguard the creation and registration of electronic lasting powers of attorney, or LPAs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Currently, only hard copies of LPAs are accepted.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: MSF, as the domain Ministry, will partner other Government agencies and community touchpoints to assist those who are less digitally-savvy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: MSF will also engage the relevant professional groups to ensure effective implementation of the electronic LPA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In general, with all the domains and the specific documents and concerns, the Ministries will undertake consultation with stakeholders and ensure that even as we seek to realise the benefits of digitalisation, appropriate safeguards are put in place to foster the trust that is pivotal to the success of these moves.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As we step up our digitalisation efforts, it is also understandable that there will naturally be concerns about new types of risks and fraud in going digital.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is by no means unique to the digital domain.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We know that fraud and other risks exist even in the physical domain.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Transferable documents or instruments, such as bills of lading, are largely for commercial use.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have already covered in quite some detail the legal and technological safeguards which will protect businesses and strengthen trust in the use of ETRs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These apply to safeguards for individuals as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We do recognise that documents or instruments are used differently, depending on the specific context and use cases, which means safeguards will need to be calibrated or tailored to the situation as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: MCI, IMDA and sector agencies are, therefore, adopting a phased approach, where items from the Exclusion List will be removed only when the relevant supporting legislative and regulatory frameworks and corresponding safeguards are in place.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This approach will, first, provide clarity to businesses and individuals on requirements needed to use such documents electronically and, second, ensure adequate safeguards are put in place to protect the vulnerable and less digitally-savvy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I agree with Ms Joan Pereira on the importance of ensuring that our less digitally comfortable citizens do not inadvertently experience greater inconvenience as we step up our digitalisation efforts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: My colleagues and I at MCI accord utmost importance to digital inclusivity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why the ETA does not, for a start, mandate the use of electronic documents or the electronic medium for transactions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Instead, the ETA enables electronic transactions as an additional option and provides a clear legal framework to recognise and support these transactions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As such, it does not remove individuals’ option to receive communications and to transact through non-electronic means.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Similarly, businesses are free to weigh the costs and benefits and decide for themselves if they wish to invest in adopting ETR solutions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Currently, section 5 of the ETA already provides for party autonomy and makes clear that the use of electronic forms of documents or instruments is not compulsory.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, again, at the business level, there is flexibility.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: While providing the flexibility of options to businesses and individuals is important, we need to also ensure that Singaporeans keep pace with technology, not just for economic reasons or for the sake of technology in itself, but to enhance their quality of life and to fully derive the benefits that can be realised through the use of technology.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It ensures that our laws continue to facilitate businesses’ use of new technologies while ensuring that we remain interoperable with the global trade economy, reinforcing Singapore’s status as a maritime and financial hub.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But there are many other sectors that can benefit greatly from digitalisation.
